rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention and resolution pattern will identify critical pairs and guide window trimming.

Halve the gradient slope while holding solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to identify which crowded pairs respond to slope. The first run's early elution leaves room to spread peaks without a large time penalty.
Keep the shallower gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity at the remaining unresolved pair. Higher temperature should also shorten retention and reduce the time penalty.
Test an intermediate temperature to separate the pair that coelutes at 60 C while retaining the selectivity improvement over 40 C. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature effects.

At 60 C only one pair remains unresolved, and its unequal peak widths suggest different gradient responses. A moderately steeper gradient may split this crossing while shortening the run; the other close pair will be monitored for lost resolution.

Shorten the gradient one step to increase separation of the remaining critical pair, which improved strongly from 24 to 20 minutes. This tests whether it reaches R = 1.5 before the earlier close pairs fall below that threshold.

The best run is only slightly short of full resolution. Raising the starting organic fraction one step makes the gradient slightly shallower while shortening the initial low-organic segment, testing a nearby selectivity balance between the two limiting pairs.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 7 to improve the two early close pairs while preserving the later pair's resolution margin. The narrower solvent window should still contain all eight peaks within the gradient and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Injection 8 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction while making the gradient shallower to test a shorter fully resolved separation without sacrificing the early critical pairs.

Make the gradient shallower at the higher starting fraction to recover resolution of the early critical pair. This tests whether the later pair's resolution margin can support a faster alternative to injection 8, which remains the maximum-score benchmark.

The high-temperature branch shows a tradeoff between two critical pairs, so test a cooler selectivity regime at the shallow slope used in injection 2. The higher starting organic fraction should offset some additional retention; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Lower temperature with the gradient fixed to test whether the remaining early coelution separates in the cooler regime. This also checks for a late-pair order crossing before attempting further time reduction; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.
Shorten the fully resolved 25 C gradient by one step to test its resolution margin and reduce elution time. Injection 8 remains the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Trim the low-organic portion of the cooler method while reducing its gradient slope to recover the critical pair's resolution. This tests whether the fully resolved low-temperature regime can approach injection 8's shorter elution time.

Test a steeper gradient to move the cooler method beyond the critical pair's apparent selectivity crossing and shorten elution. The other pairs have useful resolution margins; injection 8 remains the proven maximum-score method.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward while preserving the slope to test whether initial-solvent selectivity further separates the critical pair after its order reversal. This should also shorten retention, while injection 8 remains the proven maximum-score benchmark.

Shift the solvent window upward another step at the same slope, following the critical pair's improvement from R 0.59 to 1.35. This tests a substantially faster fully resolved method while monitoring the neighboring pair for convergence.
Injection 17 is now the shortest fully resolved method tested. Shorten its gradient one step to locate the speed limit, monitoring the two pairs with R near 1.6.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention, but use a shallower slope to compensate for the resolution lost with faster gradients. This tests a faster fully resolved alternative while retaining injection 17 as the benchmark.

Test whether shifting the solvent window another step moves the middle critical pair through its selectivity crossing into a faster resolved regime. Monitor the earliest pair for excessive compression; injection 17 remains the shortest proven fully resolved method.

Return to the shortest fully resolved method and raise temperature one step to test a faster separation through temperature selectivity rather than further solvent compression. Monitor the two pairs near R = 1.6; injection 17 remains the benchmark.
Test whether temperature moves the unresolved middle pair in injection 19 beyond its selectivity crossing into a faster resolved regime. Injection 17 remains the shortest proven maximum-score method.

Refine the shortest fully resolved method with a smaller slope increase than the unsuccessful eight-minute gradient. This tests whether some of injection 17's resolution margin can be exchanged for shorter retention while retaining maximum CRF.

Trim injection 17's unused gradient tail while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and slope. The last peak previously eluted near organic fraction 0.525, so this endpoint should preserve full resolution and the 4.14-minute last-peak time with a shorter programmed gradient.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower gradient for greater resolution margin around the fastest fully resolved regime. Injection 24 remains the shortest-programmed proven maximum-score method; this alternative may offer more robust separation with only a modest increase in retention time.
